lesson.title: What a Source Feels Like Under Load: Output Resistance
lesson.summary: Output resistance is the Thevenin resistance seen looking back into a circuit's output terminals, and it is exactly what causes a source's voltage to sag once a real load starts drawing current.
lesson.body:
Output resistance, written R_out, is the Thevenin equivalent resistance of a circuit's output port, found by the same source deactivation procedure used for any Thevenin resistance calculation: replace independent voltage sources with short circuits, independent current sources with open circuits, then find the equivalent resistance looking back into the output terminals. Every real source, a battery, a sensor, an amplifier's output stage, a signal generator, behaves like an ideal source in series with this resistance. Output resistance is simply the name given to R_th when the emphasis is on that source's role at an output port rather than on reducing a larger network.

An ideal voltage source has R_out equal to zero, and it holds its rated voltage no matter how much current a load draws from it. No real source achieves that. Every real source has some R_out greater than zero, which means its terminal voltage sags as load current increases, because part of the source's own voltage gets used up driving current through its own internal resistance rather than reaching the load.

Take a 9V battery with output resistance R_out = 3 ohm, connected to a load R_L = 6 ohm. The current is I = 9V divided by (3 ohm plus 6 ohm), or 9 divided by 9, which is 1A. The voltage actually available at the terminals is V_s minus I times R_out, or 9V minus 1A times 3 ohm, which is 6V. That matches I times R_L, or 1A times 6 ohm, also 6V, confirming the calculation.

Now compare a lighter load, R_L = 27 ohm. The current is 9V divided by 30 ohm, or 0.3A, and the terminal voltage is 9V minus 0.3A times 3 ohm, or 9V minus 0.9V, which is 8.1V, much closer to the ideal, unloaded value of 9V. As the load resistance grows large relative to R_out, the terminal voltage climbs back toward the open circuit value, exactly the same pattern seen from the opposite side of a connection in the input resistance chapter.

In practice, the output resistance of a real source can be found experimentally by comparing its open circuit voltage to its voltage under a known load and solving for R_out algebraically, or it can be calculated directly using the same deactivate the sources, look into the terminals procedure used for any Thevenin resistance. This value is precisely what the load resistance chapter's voltage divider depends on, and it is one half of the picture, together with input resistance, that the loading effect chapter completes next.

Running that experimental method on the 9V, 3 ohm example confirms the relationship works in reverse too. Measure the open circuit voltage first, with nothing connected: it reads 9V, since with no load current flowing there is no drop across R_out at all. Then connect the known 6 ohm load and measure again: it reads 6V, exactly as calculated. Solving V_s minus I times R_out equals V_loaded for R_out, using I equal to the loaded voltage divided by the load resistance, or 6V divided by 6 ohm, which is 1A, gives R_out equal to (9V minus 6V) divided by 1A, or 3 ohm, recovering the same value the circuit was built with. This two measurement technique is exactly how a real, unlabeled source's output resistance gets characterized on a workbench, without ever needing to open it up and inspect its internal wiring directly.
